Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, on a
Old Age Pensions

question of privilege, I desire to call attention to the following statement in an editorial on Canadian National Railways appearing in this morning's Ottawa Journal:
It is nonsense, for example, and not quite honest, for Mr. Dunning to point out as an illustration of the system's success that only ten millions of the fifty millions that parliament voted for the road last year was actually used, when almost in the next breath it had to be shown that the reason for this was simply that the railway raised some 45 millions on bond issues guaranteed by the government-and for which the country is responsible.
The reference quoted contains a rather serious misapprehension of the facts, which I feel sure is quite unintentional on the part of the Journal, and which the Journal will be foremost in desiring to set right.
The 50 millions of which only 10 were actually required of the government, were voted for the fiscal year 1925-26. The 35 millions, raised by guarantee of bonds, was part of the vote of the previous fiscal year 1924-25 and, while falling within the scope of the calendar year covered by Sir Henry Thornton's report, formed no part of my presentation of the railway estimates which were, of course, for the fiscal year 1926-27 as contrasted with the fiscal years 1925-26. The error arises, of course, from the fact that the accounts of the railways are on the basis of the calendar year while those of the government are on the basis of the federal fiscal year. This I was careful to explain when dealing with these figures. There were no bond issues, guaranteed or otherwise, during the fiscal year 1925-26.

speechtext: Oh absolutely.

What is the
definition of a criminal offence as contained in part II of the Criminal Code referred to in this bill? The reason I ask is that this reprinted bill seems very different in character and in scope from bill 91. That bill provides:
Whenever any alien advocates in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Great Britain or Canada, or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or the overthrow by force or violence of constituted law and authority, or assassination, or shall by word or act create or attempt to create riot or public disorder in Canada, or shall by common repute belong to or be suspected of belonging to any secret society or organization which extorts money from, or in any way attempts to control any resident of Canada by force or threat of bodily harm, or by blackmail;
And so on. I should think that such a person is just as dangerous an individual or class of individual as a person convicted under the Criminal Code, and why the restriction? It appears to me it is a restrictive section, and why?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For the
very simple reason that it places the constitutional authority to act entirely in the hands of the minister. The old section 41 gave very wide powers to the minister to seize and deport individuals for a number of causes, and during the war it was necessary.

Is the new section 41 merely
a more succinct and briefer way of comprehending all the offences included in the old section 41, or are any of the offences
under the old section 41 omitted from the new section, and if so which?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I say very
frankly that I think, and have always thought, that the officials of the Department of Immigration should not be police officers. However the act has so fixed it. Section 41, which we are discussing to-day, simply brings to the attention of the Department of Immigration the conviction of any individual who is liable to deportation and whom the officers of the crown will have the authority to deport. It puts the matter in the hands of the police, rather than in the hands of the officials of the Immigration department. There it is however at present and this amendment is simply for the purpose of bringing these convictions to our notice. Now we propose to cancel section 41; it will go out of existence. Under the old section 41, without conviction at all, the minister could take action and deport. The minister will no longer be able to deport persons without trial-that is what it means- but the minister will still be the police officer for deportation purposes.

The answer of the minister
has not dealt with the question I raised. There are two elements in the problem. One is the offences in respect to which the machinery provided by the section is to operate; the other is the particular machinery which is to operate. The minister's reply has dealt entirely with the machinery. I am not concerned with the machinery now, but I am asking the question, whatever the machinery, whether the old or the new, what offences does it deal with? Does it deal with offences under old section 41 or only with some of them? In respect of the offences, and not the machinery, is there any difference between the old section and the one that is intended to take its place?
Mr.	STEWART	(Edmonton):	No	there
would not be. It deals with the same offences with this single exception, that the Minister of Immigration could not lay violent hands on an individual until he was tried.

All the present offences are
there with the addition of this provision?
Mr.	STEWART	(Edmonton):	Yes	they
are still offences.
Mr.	EDWARDS	(Frontenac):	The	minister has shown a disposition to answer the questions which have been put to him very fairly,	but I think his answers	indicate a
lack of knowledge of the provisions of this bill and the changes in section 41, which leads me to believe that the minister would be
Long Term Farm Loans

well advised if he accepted the suggestion made by the hon. member for Fort William.
This is an important matter.
4 p.m. The very fact that it has been dealt with on five or six occasions in this chamber shows that it is advisable to spend a little more time on it, so that we con compare the section now submitted with the old section. I think it should be laid over.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I move that the committee rise report progress and ask leave to sit again. If any hon. members who are not here to-day are interested in this perhaps hon. members would direct their attention to the bill as reprinted.

I would like the minister to
consider a slight amendment to this section. The closing part of the section contains very much the same language as the closing part of old section 41, and that language is $uite applicable to the old section, because that does not contemplate a conviction at all. It merely states that persons who do certain things shall be reported to the minister. In section 41 you are dealing with a conviction and not a complaint, and no fewer than three officers will be required to send in full particulars-first, the officer cognizant of the offence who, I suppose, would be the police constable; secondly, the official of the municipality who would be the justice of the peace or the magistrate trying the case; and, thirdly, the clerk of the municipality. It seems to me ridiculous that three different officers should be called upon to send in full particulars, and I would suggest that the minister amend the bill to make it the duty of one person, the magistrate or any other judicial officer to submit a copy of the conviction.

I do not as a rule insist
very strongly on an absolute adherence to technicalities, but I do think that in the interests of a proper observance of the rules of the House the procedure which is being followed in this instance should not go unchallenged. With all deference to the law officers, I cannot see how a bill consisting solely of one clause can be completely redrafted after it has been once introduced and then taken up in committee without reintroduction. Surely the introduction of the original bill cannot be considered as having introduced a bill which is virtually different. Personally I would offer no objection to the bill in its present form being formally introduced now, and I do not think that the House would object.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understood that the present procedure would be in order but I shall inquire further into the point and ask the indulgence of the House to allow me to introduce the bill and go right on with the consideration of it.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I did not get the amendment proposed1 by my hon. friend (Mr. Boys).

The minister in this section is providing that three officers shall submit certain particulars. I think it would be well to make it incumbent upon one person, say the magistrate, to send to the minister a copy of the conviction which is registered.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall consider the suggestion.
Progress reported.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That there shall be a board known as the Canadian Farm Loan Board which shall be a body politic and corporate consisting of four members, one of whom shall be the Minister of Finance and the other three shall be appointed by the Governor in Council and of the latter one shall be designated by the Canadian Farm Loan Commissioners.
That the board shall issue farm loan bonds to make long term loans to farmers, and the government of Canada shall provide initial capital for the board to an amount not exceeding five million dollars and subscribe an amount of 5 per cent of the capital stock as loans are made by the board.
The government of each province in which loans are made shall be required to subscribe to the capital stock of the board as loans are made in such province an amount equal to 5 per cent of the said loans and each borrower an amount of 5 per cent of his loan payable at the time the loan is made. The loans shall be made on the security of first mortgage on farm lands; the interest rate shall be such a rate in excess of the interest payable on the farm loan bonds as is sufficient to provide for the expenses of operation; the farm loan bonds shall be legal investments and may be purchased by the Minister of Finance provided that the amount of such bonds held by him shall not at any time exceed $15,000,000; and the amount of any payment by the government of Canada on account of capital of the board or as payment for farm loan bonds purchased shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund on the authority of the Governor in Council.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Duff in the chair.

They will market their own
bonds.

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend section 262 of the Railway Aot, 1919, and to provide that the total amount of money to be apportioned and payable from any annual appropriation shall not, in the case of any one rail level orossing, exceed forty per cent of the cost of the actual construction- work, and shall not, in any such case, exceed the sum of twenty-five thousand dollars.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, (Mr. Duff in the chair.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: This money comes out of a special fund, does it not?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: What is the amount available each year, or is there any limitation?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: The Railway Act provides for a grant of $200,000 per year for ten consecutive years, from April 1, 1919, to be applied as set out in the act. It might possibly be well to explain at this stage that the government has received many representations to the effect that on account of the relative smallness of the Dominion's contribution from this fund the use for which it was designed has been very little availed of during recent years. The Good Roads Association of Canada has been particularly urgent in its representations. The subject was referred to the Board of Rail-ways Commissioners for a report, and after examining it the board thoroughly recommends the provision contained in the resolution. Briefly, it is to the effect that the Dominion's contribution shall be increased from 25 per cent to 40 per cent, with a maximum of $25,000 for a level crossing instead of $15,000 as heretofore.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Would the
minister tell us how much has been expended for the last four or five years?
Railway Act Amendment

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: The appropriation under the act is the same annually, $200,000.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Then is it quite plain from the amendment that this will apply to individual crossings, and not to works which contain more than one crossing? It has sometimes been said with regard to section 262 of the Railway Act that the contribution should be limited to a work, and not to any individual crossing in a work.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I think, Mr
Chairman, the minister would be well advised to make that point clear. Very often in cities it is not a question of one crossing but of a big scheme which gets rid perhaps of a dozen crossings. My recollection is that there was difficulty in dealing with it at certain times.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend mean there would be a combination of several crossings in one?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
In one scheme. Take, for example, Edmonton, where my hon. friend is familiar with the layout. When we started to straighten out things we found a whole lot of crossings had to be considered at the same time, and the point was taken- I forget whether by the Department of Finance or of Railways-that you could only give aid for one particular crossing, although a whole lot of different crossings might be involved in the one work. I think the minister might well look into that. The resolution contains the phrase, "in the case of anv one rail level crossing." The proper thing to do
Mr. J. W. Edwards.]
is to get rid of the level crossing altogether and put a bridge, tunnel or something else in place of it. The original idea was to aid the elimination of grades, and to make safe highway and railway crossings. I do not think the word "level" comes in there very happily, but the minister can take that up with his legal advisers.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I quite agree that the right thing would be either a subway or a bridge, but I am afraid that is impossible in every case. In the meantime we should make the crossings as safe as possible. I did not understand the purpose of this resolution because, as I have said before, we at the other end of the House sometimes do not know what is going on until the next day. I am afraid to come over on this side too often-

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: You probably belong there.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: [DOT]-because my hon. friends opposite get a good deal of amusement when I sit over here, and I do not like to give them any more amusement than I can.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Why not come on this side?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: That would be all right too. I would like to emphasize the necessity of making level crossings safe in every possible way. I will admit that they are out of date, but under the circumstances it is impossible to have bridges and subways, so the only thing to do is make the level crossings as safe as possible.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I presume the minister has the Railway Act before him; I do not recall the provisions of section 262, and if it is not too long perhaps he might read it.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I am just trying to clear up the point as to the number of crossings; if hon. members will permit I will try to deal with each question as it comes up.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I wish hon. members would speak a little louder; we cannot hear what they say.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I will try tc remember. The definition of a crossing is dealt with in the act of 1909, subsection 5 of section 7, as follows:
"Crossing", for the purposes of this section, means any steam railway crossing of a highway, or highway crossing of a steam railway, at rail level, and every manner of construction of the railway or of the highway v the elevation or the depression of thr

Railway Act Amendment
one above or below the other, or by the diversion of the one or the other, and any other work ordered by the board to be provided as one work of protection, safety and convenience for the public in respect of one or more railways not exceeding four tracks in all crossing or so crossed.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I know the definition, and the point has been raised that When you are combining several grade crossings in one work ordered by one order of the Board of Railway Commissioners you may only ask for a contribution from the annual appropriation for the whole work and not for each crossing, although the work may contain ten crossings. For instance, the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) mentioned the city of Edmonton, where there was a separation of grades throughout part of the city. That took care of several crossings, and each of these crossings should receive its contribution if, in the view of the board, it is a proper case. The board should not be limited to $25,000 in respect of a whole work, but only in respect of each separation of grades, that is each highway crossing.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I will be glad to give consideration to that point, although part of it would appear to be covered by the provision that no such money shall in any one year be applied to more than six crossings on any one railway in any one municipality, or more than once in any one year to any one crossing.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: That is true, but the definition confuses a work with a crossing. If the minister would be good enough to consider that matter with his legal advisers the point might be cleared up.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I will be glad to consider it.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister a question. I entirely agree with the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), that these crossings should be made as safe a3 possible. Let us suppose a municipality makes a request to the Board of Railway Commissioners for the elimination of a level crossing. Does the Board of Railway Commissioners apportion the cost of such work as between the municipality and the railway on the one hand, and in relation to the 40 per cent paid by the government, on the other?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Not to exceed 40 per
cent.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Then is the
apportionment of the other 60 per cent entirely within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners as between the municipality and the railway company?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: That is the position.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: And the 40 per cent is also dealt with by the board.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Yes, but the board's authority to order payment from the con-soldiated fund is limited to 40 per cent.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Then the board, in its judgment, might give 30 per cent or 20 per cent, but not over 40 per cent?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
That is right. Sometimes the province comes into the matter also, as hon. members who are familiar with the operations of the act know. Now someone has asked me to read section 262:
(1) The sums appropriated and set apart to aid actual construction work for 'the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of highway crossings of railways at rail level in existence on the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and nine, shall be placed to the credit of a special account to be known as "The Railway Grade Crossing Fund", and shall be applied by the board subject to the limitations hereinafter set out, solely towards the cost (not including that of maintenance and operation), of actual construction work for the purpose aforesaid.
Then comes subsection (2) which we are now amending, which deals with the proportions, and then subsection (3) goes on:
In case any province contributes towards the said fund, the board may apportion, direot and order payment out of the amount so contributed by such province, subject to any conditions and restrictions made and imposed by such province in respect of its contribution.
Apparently none of the provinces have made use of that privilege, because so far as I know they have not contributed anything towards this fund. Then subsection (4) is as follows:
In this section,-
"crossing", means any steam railway crossing of a highway, or highway crossing of a steam railway, at rail level, and every manner of construction of the railway or of the highway by the elevation or the depression of the one above or below the other, or by the diversion of the one or the other, and any other work ordered by the board to be provided as one work of protection, safety and convenience for the public in respect of one or more railways not exceeding four tracks in all crossing or so crossed;
"municipality", means an incorporated city, town, village, county, township, parish, or rural municipality.
That is the whole section.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
That is the capital cost
of construction of the work. The hon.
Railway Act Amendment

member for Brandon is more interested, I think, in the safeguarding of grade crossings by the installation of a gate or a wigwag or a signal which requires maintenance from year to year, rather than by a bridge or subway. The amount attributable to construction is very slight, and the real cost is in the annual maintenance either by mechanical means or by watchmen. Sometimes three or four watchmen are required to take care of a day and night crossing. That bears rather heavily on the municipality, I happen to know, and probably my hon. friend has cases in mind in his district where the municipalities are paying heavily for that sort of protection going on from year to year. Perhaps the minister would consider authorizing the railway board to contribute some part of the annual protection cost.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot
undertake to do that. After all, we are increasing the proportion to be borne by the Dominion from 25 to 40 per cent and are increasing the maximum from $15,000 to $25,000. That is a big jump, and undoubtedly it will encourage the building of more works to eliminate level crossings than has been the case for a number of years past. I think we had better be content to move slowly and see what the effect is going to be after this present enlargement of the Dominion's contribution, before we undertake anything in the way of looking after maintenance. I am afraid that it would run into a very great deal of money if any provision were to be made for that. I think the hon. member for West York has probably more information on this matter than any other member of the House, and I would appreciate his view on the suggestion of providing at this time something additional for maintenance cost, as well as for the original cost of construction.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
There is no
doubt about it that the real cost in connection with protection of level crossings is the maintenance. H you are going to put in gates-I do not know what the cost is now, but once you could put in pretty good gates for $2,500 or $3,000. If you have a more complicated layout, it may cost double that amount, or a little more when you have something else tied up with it, but the gates as gates are not very expensive to install originally. Nevertheless, even in the old days, putting in gates had the effect of creating a capital carrying charge of $50,000. What I mean by that is that it took at least the interest on $50,000 to look after the mainten-
ance of those gates, watchmen, the supply of oil. and the like. It would cost even more now I should think-I have not looked at the figures for a long time-and that is quite a burden on the municipalities.
But in justice to the minister I have to admit that the underlying idea of the act was the elimination of crossings more than anything else. At the same time there is this practical thing we have to remember. The step that is now being taken is wise. We never gave enough to crossing elimination before; we were simply playing with it, but even with what we are now doing we are not going to have very many more crossing eliminations. Grade eliminations to-day run to a great deal of money. Subways and bridges are very, very expensive. Most of them cost a great deal more than $15,000, which is the maximum contribution to-day, I understand.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: It will be $25,000 under this amendment.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: That helps quite materially, but what I think the minister might well do is to have just a little addition made to his resolution, which would not throw much burden at all on the government, but which would help the municipalities very materially in the construction of new gates. I think the most we could contribute from the grade crossing fund towards the cost for a gate protection-of course, this is a recollection of a great many years standing-was $200. For the ordinary level crossing protection, where there is no grade separation and the like, I think in such cases we might have a maximum not exceeding say $1,000 or $1,500 per crossing.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I do not get my hon.
friend's point.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: In cases where the whole cost mostly is maintenance rather than construction, I am suggesting that the maximum contribution which might be made from the grade crossing fund be say $1,000 or $1,500, or something like that. That would really help in the case of level crossings where the necessary money, owing to the position of the municipality and the railway, cannot be obtained for the purpose of putting in a subway or a bridge. Increasing the maximum would make it just that much more easy and render it more probable that we would have proper protection, watchmen and the like, without involving us in an annual contribution which might run into a great deal of money.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
The object I had in
mind, Mr. Chairman, in bringing this forward at all was to forward the original objective

Railway Act Amendment
of the legislation, which is the elimination of the level crossing, by increasing the amount which could be attributed by the Dominion to $25,000 per crossing. I regard it as much more advantageous to the people that the crossing should be eliminated than that we should encourage the installation of gates to a greater extent than now exists. I shall be glad to give consideration to the last suggestion made by the hon. member for West York, although it occurs to me offhand that, with the many thousands of level crossings in Canada, such an increase might result in our general fund being depleted in providing for maintenance along the line suggested.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: Not maintenance.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Well, a contribution
towards installation. In that connection may I say that the board can now order up to 40 per cent of the installation.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
But not if
the installation exceeds $2,000.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
The contribution then
would be about $900.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
NRY DRAYTON:	But we know
that both the municipality and the railway will have to go on paying two or three or four thousand dollars a year for all time.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
The real objection I
have to that is that it is rather an abandonment of the objective of the law. It is substituting the encouragement of level crossings guarded by gates for what the legislation was obviously intended in the first place to bring about, and that was, through assistance, the complete elimination of level crossings. However, I shall be glad to have the matter further looked into from the point of view my hon. friend has taken.	.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
We might as
well be absolutely frank with ourselves. We shall never entirely eliminate level crossings. It cannot be done. speechtext:
I am not sure the minister has understood my question. I will read from the resolution as it is here:
The total amount of money to be apportioned and payable from any annual appropriation shall not, in the case of any one rail level crossing, exceed 40 per cent of the cost of the actual construction work, and shall not, in any such case, exceed the sum of $25,000.
Now three level crossings were eliminated by the diversion. Would the contribution be limited to $25,000 or to $75,000? One of these diversions cost the highways board of the province of Nova Scotia something in the vicinity of $150,000. The other one costs less, but both of them cut out three level crossings on which accidents had occurred resulting in great damage to the rolling stock of the railway. I would be very glad if the minister could raise the amount both in the case of the 40 per cent and as to the sum total of $25,000. An enormous number of people are being killed every year and that number is unfortunately increasing. Therefore, any money which can be expended in preventing accidents of this kind is surely justified. The highways were created before the railways came into existence, and bearing that fact in mind the railways should assume at least one-half the cost of making diversions which will not only give more protection to the public, but will also protect railway property.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I should like to bring to
the attention of the committee a matter that has been on my mind for some little time. I believe that if a slight and very inexpensive addition were made to the signs placed at railway crossings a good many accidents might be prevented. The necessity of this was brought very forcibly to my attention
Railway Act Amendment

last summer, when a very sad accident occurred near the town where I reside. Perhaps if I described this accident hon. members could better get my point of view. A family of five, on their way to the exhibition at Regina came up to a railway crossing where there was a double track, a fact of which they were not aware. A long freight was proceeding westerly, and they waited for it to pass. Immediately that freight passed the automobile driver pulled up onto the track. But a short freight was proceeding eastward at the same time,, the sight of which was hidden from the driver's view by the long freight. Apparently the engineer of the short freight blew the whistle as required by law, but the engines being close together the driver of the motor thought it was the engine of the train he was watching. The result was that he got on the track. The east bound freight was only about forty yards away and travelling at a fast rate. It struck the car and two of the occupants were so badly injured that they died within an hour or two. Two others were seriously injured, and a fifth person escaped with a few scratches. I asked the driver afterwards, when he was in the hospital recovering, this question:	Had there been some additional
sign denoting that the track was a double one would not some of the occupants of the car have noticed it with the result that the accident would not have taken place? The injured man told me that he felt certain such would have been the case. It seems to me that if some additional device carrying the word "double," in a different colour, or perhaps in red letters, were placed above the present sign "railway crossing" so that it would read "double railway crossing," a good many accidents would be prevented. It would cost very little because it would only need to be placed where there was a double track crossing. Recently I was informed that a similar accident took place in western Ontario, but I failed to notice it in the paper and could not find out exactly where it happened. There is nothing to indicate at these crossings that there is a double track, or that there are three tracks, and many people who are accustomed to driving across single track are apt to forget the danger. I should like to point out that in the particular instance I spoke of the west bound freight was right in front of the people sitting in the car and thus prevented them from seeing the second track on the other side. That is all I wish to say in connection with this matter, but I hope the minister will seriously consider the representations made.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919 AMENDMENT FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO ELIMINATION OF LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext: May I just remark that accidents of this kind seem to me tc indicate very clearly the necessity not of more signs, but of having crossings which make such accidents impossible. 1 do not think that level crossings can be justified simply because of their cheapness or a sufficiency of signs. I should like to look at this matter not merely from the standpoint of people who are travelling in motor cars, but also from the point of view of the railway employees, I know that representations have been made again and again to the government by railway employees as to the dangers which exist at level crossings. These employees are under a very great strain constantly in trying to be on the lookout for possible traffic when they should be attending to their engines or to other duties. It seems to me that these representations, made by men who are daily brought into contact with the possibility of accidents, ought to be listened to, and the comparatively small expenditure involved ought not to stand in the way of taking adequate measures for the protection of human life.

Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

and to make provision for <the improvement, management and regulation of the harbour of Chicoutimi, in the province of Quebec.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Duff in the chair.

Before the resolution is
carried, I am interested to know something about it in a general way. We have harbour commissions at Quebec, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, and I should like to know why one is required at Chicoutimi?

It is proposed to incorporate the Chicoutimi Harbour Commissioners, more particularly in view of the development which is taking place in lake St. John and vicinity. The Chicoutimi harbour is somewhat important at the present time. Chicoutimi has a population of nearly 10,000, and in view of the development taking place in that district, it has been found necessary to place the harbour of Chicoutimi under the jurisdiction of a hatbour commission.

been spent on the harbour there?

I could not say. It has
been under the Department of Public Works.

I do not want to appear
in the position of opposing the measure, but I want information. The minister says it is necessary, and it struck me as strange. There are a great many harbours on the Great Lakes where the government has spent millions of dollars and where there are no harbour commissions. The development at Chicoutimi is pulp and paper is it not?
No, aluminum.

I cannot imagine that one industry at Chicoutimi would make the harbour compare with the harbours on the Great Lakes where they are handling coal. I have no objection personally however. What is the intention of the government in regard to the harbour commission? Is there any hope of it being self-supporting?
We hope it will be.
From dues collected in the harbour?
Yes.

Is there anything in the
bill which will be based on the resolution providing for expenses?

The expenses will be met
by the harbour commission.

Chicoutimi Harbour Commission

But the commission will
have no money until it is collected by them. Will there be any advances by the government?
No.

We must not
assume too quickly that the minister is 100 per cent right. He is not asking for any advance this session, but next session or the following session he will be asking for it. It will be just the same as Three Rivers. Does my hon. friend remember the nice discussion we had when Three Rivers wanted to get a commission, and our genial friend, who is now in another chamber, was very much in favour of it? I think he found that it was a regular nuisance. We know there is the matter of necessity. Somebody wants a job in connection with the harbour commission. It is a great necessity sometimes to supply the job.

was always able to withstand the pressure. We never incorporated one harbour commission while I was in office. My hon. friend is not quite so successful in that respect as I fortunately was. People want patronage here and jobs there all over the country, and every now and again the government falls for it. No.

What is the
real necessity?

We believed that the affairs of the port could be administered to better advantage by a commission in close contact with the harbour at Chicoutimi and familiar with the conditions there. We
5 p.m. thought that preferable to sending someone from the department down there to look after the affairs of this port. I am quite sure the harbour is going to take care of itself, in view of the development, as Three Rivers has done. mentis will take place around lake St. John, and if later on they come to parliament asking for any assistance they will probably be in a position to show that they are capable of paying interest on the money we may advance to them. Unquestionably it is legitimate so long as it does not involve the people of Canada in any expense. Take for instance one of the most important harbours in the whole Dominion, a harbour through which probably more freight is shipped than through Montreal, even. I refer to the head of the lakes, were 80 or 90 per cent of the grain of western Canada is handled, not to mention coal going west and all package freight westbound which does not go via the Panama canal. That harbour is immense and some $14,000,000 has been spent on it; yet there has never been a harbour commission there. It is obvious therefore that very much can be done without the assistance of a commission. of Chicoutimi?
I have not the figures under my hand, but I shall give them when the bill is before the committee.

Unless the revenue were substantial I should not think this would be a paying proposition, and if it is to be made at all appreciable there will be imposed on those using the wharves an additional burden.

vicinity.

represent the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay and not Chicoutimi.

REPORT OF BOARD OF INTERNAL ECONOMY- MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Before the House proceeds with the next order of business I desire by unanimous leave to read the report which I have prepared in consequence of a meeting of the Board of Internal Economy this morning:
With regard to the complaints arising out of the action of the Sergeant-at-Arms in taking means to prevent theft in the members' rooms, the matter was brought before the Board of Internal Economy this morning.
After hearing Colonel Bowie's explanation and considering his memorandum, the board was of opinion that he acted in good faith, his sole object being to protect the property of members. Since 'the opening of the session, different objects, and sometimes money, have disappeared from desks in the members' rooms. It is a well known fact that there are several keys for each room, some of which are for the char service and secretaries, messengers and .pages. A patrol has always been carried out for fire protection and other services such as heating, light, et cetera. The emergency order given by the Sergeant-at-Arms on May 1st was not, as has been stated, for the purpose of raiding liquor in the rooms. The law allows anyone to have liquor in his possession, provided it is obtained legally or purchased from an authorized vendor.
It was because of several complaints that the above order was given. Unfortunately it was not written and the officer to whom it was intrusted, instead of carrying it out himself, with proper caution, passed it on to a subordinate who, in turn, gave it to another constable. The men who made the search found, in unlocked desks, several objects besides liquor, which they labelled and took over to the constables' quarters.
In view of the wrong impression caused 'by this urgent measure of protection, I 'have given instruction, after consulting my colleagues of the Board of Economy that, in future, none but the usual patrol will take place and members will have to accept the responsibility for the safeguarding of their personal effects in their desks and filing cabinets.
A fictitious and libellous list has been circulated purporting to give the names of .the members in whose rooms the effects were found. The Royal Canadian

Mounted Police has been requested to inquire as to how it originated.
. Action will be taken as soon as the report is received.
Undue importance was given to this incident which, after all, was nothing but a measure of protection unfortunately magnified and aggravated by the circumstance that it seemed connected with .the infraction of the temperance act.
Regarding the claim of extra territoriality raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) as applied to parliament buildings, it is a very big question which requires careful study and consideration. I may, however, state in a general way that the immunities, rights and privileges of parliament are of immemorial standing and, according to Anson, page 153, it has always been admitted by the courts that the House has the exclusive right "to regulate its own internal concerns."
I think this will put an end to an incident that, as I say, has been unduly magnified.

The House in committee of Supply, Mr. Duff in the chair.
Miscellaneous-amount required for remission of excise tax paid on automobiles remaining in the hands of dealers and unsold, at the time when such tax was repealed by order in council, December 18, 1920, P.C. 1/3163, $1,690,000.
Hon. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise):	Mr. Chairman, this
item was inserted for the purpose of remitting to the automobile dealers of Canada the luxury tax which they had paid to the Dominion government in 1930, when the tax was removed by order in council without any effective provision having been made to recoup the dealers for the amount which they had paid to the Dominion government, but which they had not yet collected through the sale of their cars. I think the matter is well understood by the House, a very elaborate statement, I am informed, having been prepared by the Retail Automobile Dealers' Association of Canada and mailed to every hon member. I understand there is unanimity concerning this refund. I am quite willing to answer any questions as to the number of cars or the amount of the claims. It might perhaps be well to place upon Hansard a short history of the reason for the refund.
At the commencement the minister might say why the government delayed so long in making this refund.	.

For the same reason that my hon. friends who sit on the other side of the House delayed making the refund from the date the order in council was passed in December, 1920, until they went out of power in 1921, a year later.

Supply-Customs and Excise
We had but one year.
What was tha1 reason?

I am informed that it was an effort to arrange a settlement between the automobile dealers and the automobile manufacturers under a certain verbal agreement which had been entered into between their respective representatives at the time the luxury * tax was removed. That agreement was never carried out.
By whom?

By the manufacturers. In justice to my right hon. friend and to the members of his cabinet I have just stated that they attempted to settle the matter by [DOT]getting the manufacturers to indemnify the dealers when the tax was repealed The present government endeavoured to adjust the matter in the same way without drawing upon the federal treasury.
There are two questions involved. The first is, Shall the refund be made? I think everyone is agreed that this should be done. The refund will be made by the government to those parties who paid the tax, but it will be safeguarded in such a manner that that portion of the refund which has not been made up by the manufacturer to the retailer will eventually reach the retailer who paid the tax.
The other question relates to interest. The sum included in the estimate is sufficiently large to repay the entire amount oi the taxes paid on all automobiles in the dealers' hands which were unsold on December 20, 1920, amounting to $1,2150,000. It is estimated that the interest upon that represents approximately the balance of $440,000.
The refund, of course, is more or less of a compassionate allowance, because it is admitted by all that the government which imposed the taxation had a right tc remove it, but the removal of the luxury tax, which was asked for by the automobile manufacturers of Canada, certainly caused a real hardship to the dealers. The total number of dealers affected and who submitted claims for a refund is 1,504. The lowest loss sustained by any dealer was $69.30. excluding interest to daite. The highest loss of any dealer was $19,012.98; the average loss per dealer was approximately $833.33, and the total number of cars included in the claims was 7,503. The Canada Motor Car Company of Toronto has gone into liquidation and its business is being wound up. The
liquidator of the concern has submitted a claim on behalf of the company and the creditors will, of course, get the benefit of the refund when it is made.
What is the refund in that case?

I am afraid I cannot give
that information to my hon. friend. I do not think I have the names of the individual dealers. It is not the practice of the department to give the amount due any particular person or partnership, and while I could give the amounts by provinces, the number of dealers, and the amount of the claims in each particular province, I am afraid I cannot give any individual names and amounts. I would have no objection to doing so in this particular case, but I do not happen to have the information.
Will the minister say how he proposes to deal with the case where the autombbile manufacturer made certain refunds to the dealer?

Yes. That matter has been arranged through the good offices of Mr. James R. Dixon of Ottawa; two different powers of attorney have been drawn up whereby he has been authorized to represent both the manufacturers and the dealers. The manufacturer makes proof of the amount of money remitted to each individual dealer and the dealer makes proof of the amount of money paid and of the number of oars on hand in each particular case. The amount of money paid by any manufacturer to any dealer who had cars on hand will be paid to the manufacturer, and the balance will be paid to the dealers.
Is it necessary to pay interest on these claims?

No. I made the amount in the estimates large enough to pay the interest, but as I said before this is more or less in the form of a compassionate allowance; it is an amount paid to men who have suffered, but who I could Say have suffered "legally." They could not complain of the law; they could not take an action against the government; it is a claim in equity and a claim in justice, but iit is not a claim in law. My understanding is that in all countries where allowances of this kind are paid the interest is not included. On the other hand there has been great delay and it may work a serious hardship to these men if interest is not
Supply-Customs and Excise

paid. I made the amount sufficiently large to cover interest. I would welcome to-night the opinions of hon. members on both sides of the House as to whether or not interest should be paid.

I remember this circumstance quite well, Mr. Chairman; it is a circumstance such as may arise at any time in the event of the removal of an excise tax. The only dangerous feature of this case is the precedent which will be set. I realize there is very great merit in the claim; of course it is not a legal claim and could never be established in law, but that the men lost the money I think there is no doubt. An excise tax is removed which they have paid prior to sale, as indeed must always be the case; then on the removal of that tax they are unable to collect it because of the competition of goods not Subject to the excise; they cannot possibly collect it, and the money is simply lost. I know the government could not be compelled to pay interest; this is what one might call a grant in misericordia, but if there is a claim for the principal the claim for the interest would be just as strong, and I do not see why it should be denied.
The removal of the excise giving rise to this condition was made, I thought, a little later than the minister said, but of course I cannot recall the exact month. The claim -was made some time later, and was very carefully considered at the time. The government of the day were confronted with the difficuty I have just stated; they were quite aware that in the future remissions of excise would inevitably be made and consequently feared to recognize claims of that kind because the precedent might lead us into paths very far-reaching indeed. As a matter of fact it might possibly reach into a sphere other than the removal of excise and the consequences that flow therefrom; however, I do not need to traverse that at the moment. So we started to work to find some method of getting the loss adjusted without calling upon the treasury of the country, and succeeded in having an arrangement arrived at. I am sorry the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) is not here, because he was chiefly instrumental in making the arrangement between the manufacturers on the one hand and the dealers on the other. For some reason which I do not even yet understand that arrangement was not carried through. The minister says the manufacturers failed to carry out their part of the agreement, and I accept his statement.

Could I interject just a
word? It has been reported to me by the officials of the department that, as my hon. friend has stated, at the request of the hon. member for West York, who was then Minister of Finance, the representatives of dealers and of manufacturers came together at Ottawa and arrived at an understanding by which the manufacturers would recoup to the dealers on future sales 50 per cent of the excise lost on cars which were then on hand, and add the other 50 per cent to the cost of the new cars. A great many of the dealers were overloaded with cars and were unable to dispose of the quantity required to recoup themselves during that season, and I think the manufacturers contended that the agreement did not apply to subsequent years.

I recall it quite well' now; that is the explanation. For that reason it fell through, and the falling through was not complete at the time we left office, so the matter did not come before us for reconsideration and adjustment. I am sorry there has been so much delay in coming to a solution and I am sorry that some solution was not advanced which would relieve the treasury. However, I suppose there is none possible now with the exception of this, anc for my part I support the vote.

I am in accord with the grant, but I would like to know what portion of this money is to be paid in commissions, and if it is to be paid by the department. If this is to be a real compassionate allowance I think the dealers are entitled to get the money themselves without any rake-off.

I will tell my hon. friend that the government has no knowledge of a rakeoff. I do know that Mr. Dixon of Ottawa has done a great deal of work in bringing the claims together, in getting all the dealers and manufacturers to sign the required powers of attorney and so on, but what his commission may be I have no knowledge. But I can assure my hon. friend that individual cheques will be made payable to the order of each individual dealer, and they themselves will arrange to pay their attorney. The government has no undertaking whatever to pay any commission in connection with the matter.

That is very satisfactory.
I am glad to hear the minister make that statement.

What proportion of these claims was adjusted by the manufacturers?

Supply-Customs and Excise

Eightv-five thousand dollars is to be returned direct to the manufacturers who have paid claimi to the dealers, and the balance is to be paid to the dealers themselves.
Mr. MoGIBBON: That is $85,000 of this $1,690,000?	.
Yes.
Does the minister say that $85,000 is to go to the manufacturers to recoup them for-

To recoup them for the
amount they refunded to the dealers.
After the old agreement it. seems to be pretty generous.

We felt that it would be a great hardship if we refunded the amount to the dealers and thereby gave a blanket discharge to the manufacturers who undertook to make this refund and did not live up to their obligations. We felt that the manufacturer who had really lived up to his obligation, and who had paid his proportionate share to the dealer, should be treated the same as the dealers themselves; in other words, that if we were going to remit this tax it would be unfair to reimburse some and withhold it from others; that the complete tax should be remitted, and that the manufacturer who had lived up to his agreement should not be penalized for having done so.
Who are the manufacturers who lived up to their agreement?

I cannot give the exact amount in each case, but the following Canadian motor manufacturers made reimbursement at least to a certain extent where the dealers were able to purchase new cars:
The Canadian Briscoe Motor Company.
The Chevrolet Motor Company.
The McLaughlin Moitor Company.
The Willys-Overland Company.
The Olds Motor Company of Canada.
The Maxwell Motor Company.
The Chalmers Motor Company.
The Ford Motor Company.
Mr. MEiIGHEN:	What others are left
out?

The Studebaker Company did not reimburse its dealers for any portion of the tax paid on the cars, and there were also subsidiary companies of American concerns who import cars into Canada and sell them here through dealers and distributors who made no refund.
It looks as though the Canadian manufacturers had acted quite fairly and rightly, and that the importers of American cars had not.

Yes. There was evidently an attempt on the part of these Canadian manufacturers to live up to their agreement, and I think they would have done so if the sales of cars had been sufficient. But as the dealers had on hand all the cars that they had been unable to sell, and could not take as many new cars from the Canadian manufacturers, the manufacturers only lived up to their agreements in respect to the number of new cars taken by the dealers, and that number was not large.
The American exporters to Canada made no attempt to co-operate at all?
No, apparently no attempt whatever.
There is a great lesson to be learned there.
Some of the firms the minister mentioned have passed entirely out of business.

Yes, I understand they have, but I understand that their interests have been taken over by other concerns that their claims are legally filed, and that all these firms are legally represented before the department.
Mr. MoGIBBON: I am not opposing this in the least, but I would like to point this out to the minister: Every individual purchaser who bought his car one day or a week or a few weeks before the reduction had to pay that tax, and I think it would be quite sufficiently generous on the part of this government to reimburse the dealers for the capital only, and let them go without their interest. I do not think it is fair to pay the dealer the very last dollar and let the purchaser who bought his car just a few days before suffer the complete loss. I do not think that is fair to the ultimate purchaser of the car.

The appointments were made on the request of the Minister of Finance at the time, or about the time, the Victory 'loans were started. In connection with this particular branch we found that the method has worked out so very satisfactorily in the matter of expense and collection of revenue that we thought it would be better not to interfere, but that we should leave matters as they were. It has been pointed out that a large majority of these employees have to come in contact with the tax paying public of Canada, and that the inspectors of taxation in the respective cities where these offices are established, are better judges of the men who will be able more efficiently to perform the work, meet the taxpayer, and, let me say, collect the money without trouble, without inconvenience and without recrimination on the part of the taxpayer, than if they were appointed by a Civil Service Commission sitting at Ottawa.
My hon. friend agrees with that?
I certainly do.

So do I. Therefore I do not see any reason why the same rule should not be applied in reference to other appointments, instead of having them made by the Civil Service Commission. The minister has given encouragement not only to the continuance of the employees of the Income Tax branch outside the scope of the act, but to the bedevilment of the whole civil service and of the Civil Service Act ever since his party came into power. The whole history of this government in relation to the Civil Service Act has been one of stealthy invasion from the first clause to the last and

from the first month of power to the last day. I know that as respects the employees of the Income Tax branch they were, when taken on during the regime of the late government, maintained without the operation of the act, just as were the employees of the Civil Re-establishment department. These departments were established at a time when it was believed that their duration would be quite brief, and that consequently it would not be just to the service in general to bring them within the act and make them permanent civil servants, thereby giving them a claim upon permanent occupation within the civil service of Canada. If bon. gentlemen will project their minds back to the rather hectic days when the income fax was first introduced and, as well, to the time when the Civil Re-establishment department was put on its feet, they will recall that it was the general feeling then that these were merely emergency services which it was necessary to undertake for the time being. For that reason and for no other were these employees kept without the pale of the Civil Service Act. It was not intended that they should have any claim for permanent appointment within the service. But so far as the Income Tax branch is concerned, we know quite well by this time that we shall have an income tax in Canada for years to come. This government will have gone; its memory will have become nothing but an unpleasant historic recollection, and we shall still have the income tax in this country. So that whatever reason did exist before for maintaining these employees outside the scope of the act, that reason is now removed. The government have not been satisfied to maintain the income tax employees as patronage or temporary servants outside the pale of the act, but step by step, sometimes by stealth, sometimes openly, they have yanked one branch after another from the purview of the act, occasionally by order in council removing a thousand at a stretch and, indeed, as many as 12,000. The result is that to-day one-third of the whole service is outside the act. I want to pay hon. gentlemen to my left this compliment: there would not be one line of the act in force to-day if it were not for the influence of the Progressive party. With one or two exceptions they have been opposed to these encroachments upon the act and certainly they never doubted that we would stand by the act.

Now, how long is the government going to take to collect these business profits taxes? The act imposing them 'has been repealed six or seven years. I would not suggest that any person employed in the collection of business profits taxes should be put under the Civil Service Act. Surely we will get to the end of it some day, but any little job at all seems to be a life job when it gets into the hands of this administration. They are collecting these business profits taxes yet, and I expect they will be collecting them until they pass from this earthly scene.
And there is something else they are after. I notice in the estimates an .item for the adjustment of war debts. This in our day was called demobilization. "Demobilization" was defined by the law as the "adjustment of war debts." But we were tilted at away back in 1919 and were asked to explain to parliament why it was we had not all these war debts adjusted, and we were told the reason was that we wanted to keep up the war spirit in Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite are still adjusting those war debts. They have been adjusting them now for four and a half years. They have in the estimates an item of $275,000 for the purpose. When in the name of common sense do they expect ever to get rid of those war debts? Will they be keeping them going until the next election? Is it a handy thing to adjust these debts just before an election?
But on the subject of income tax I warn the government that this country is not going to tolerate the conduct of any administration that reverses the will of the people as expressed in the Civil Service Act. Hon. members say the employees are satisfied because they get a little more. In that very fact lies one of the main reasons of the act. Unless you have one common body having under its purview all the multiplied branches of the civil service, and able to make a study and estimate the relative difficulty of the variety of duties in the various departments of government, and the relative talent required for their discharge, you are never going to have anything that approaches equity in the distribution of the salary list; you will have all kinds of anomalies and inequalities. Anomaly exists to-day, inequality exists to-day in relation to the service outside. This will become more and more rampant as the government pursues its headlong course of abolishing letter by letter, line by line and page by page the Civil Service Act. I should like the hon. minister to get the opinion of the civil servants of this city and the country generally on the course the government has pursued in relation to the act. I warn the administration that so far as my influence goes I will resist to the uttermost any further invasion of its provisions whatsoever. And I hope I can depend upon hon. gentlemen to my left-
Hear, hear.

I hope there are independent spirits enough among them, and I hope there are those who have learned enough of the character and conduct of this administration, that in this, if in nothing else, they will give me their best support.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two in regard to the Civil Service Commission. When the creation of such a commission first came before parliament I took a stand, not against it-I have not taken that stand at any time -but I contended that it was being loaded with a lot of work which could be better performed by the individual members of parliament. And I say that yet. I took the stand then, I take it to-day, that the appointment, for instance, of a country postmaster might

well be left in the hands of the member of parliament, no matter whether he sat on the government side or on this side of the House -that to leave such appointments with the Civil Service Commission was loading the commissioners with work that they were not as well qualified to perform as the members of this House, who are held responsible by their constituents for the capacity of the country postmaster who is appointed by the Civil Service Commission upon the advice of one or two persons living in the community where the postmaster resided. I have never taken a stand against the creation of the Civil Service Commission or against their doing efficient work as a 'Civil Service Commission, but I believe their work would be more efficient if a great deal of this more unimportant work were taken off their shoulders and performed by the members, who would be held responsible by their constituents for the appointments made. But my main objection to the Civil Service Commission, Mr. Chairman, is that during the last three or four years the commission hare made appointments so far as Conservative members of parliament were concerned, whereas a certain amount of patronage has been enjoyed by those who are on the other side of the House. This is not working out fairly, and as proof of that we have some 18,000 persons in the civil service to-day who were not appointed by the Civil Service Commission. I venture to say there are members sitting on the other side of this House whose recommendations were responsible for the appointment of several thousand of these people. That is where I say it is wrong; if you are going to have these appointments made by the Civil Service Commission let the commission rule all along the line; do not let the commission appoint a part of the service and allow others to be appointed under recommendations of certain favoured members who happen to support the government. With regard to the vote under consideration, this experimental work was undertaken some years ago by the department for the purpose of demonstrating what could be done in the way of dehydrating some of our fruits, particularly apples, apricots and plums, instead of adopting the ordinary evaporating system. During these two or three years we have, I think, demonstrated to the satisfaction, not of the fruit men because most of them were aware of it before, but of the consumer, the very much higher quality of dehydrated fruit, as compared with evaporated fruit. The systems are entirely different; so much so that the dehydrated fruit retains the flavour of the green fruit as compared with the almost entire lack of flavour in regular evaporated fruit. AVe have come to the time when we think we can accomplish it.
AA'ould the minister explain the difference between the processes?

The ordinary
evaporating is done through heated air. It has the effect of hardening the tissue and breaking down the cellular construction of the fruit. On the other hand, the dehydrating is carried on through a more humid atmosphere, retaining the cellular construction of the fruit. We have now reached the point where we can contract somewhat in experimental work, having demonstrated beyond any question that an important industry may be developed. Our experiments have been followed up by the establishment of two plants, one in the Okanagan valley and one in the Annapolis valley, both of which are giving entire satisfaction. But the fruit men having had pretty hard sledding ever since the war, capital has not been so plentiful; otherwise I am sure many plants would now be in operation. Certainly a great quantity of fruit which is not quite up to grade one, but which at the same time is capable of preservation, could be dehydrated. In this way a large proportion of our excess fruit could be disposed of. It is not at all true that you can take culls and produce a sound dehydrated article; the better the raw material the better will the finished product be.

In what way are animals
poisoned? The minister says they cannot pick up enough from the grass to notice the effect, so in what way do they secure enough of this poison to injure them?

When it is distributed evenly in the usual way an animal cannot possibly pick up enough to produce any bad effects, but if the material drifts with the wind or accumulates in any other way, animals having access to it may be poisoned. The ordinary distribution methods, under normal conditions, have quite demonstrated that it can have no poisonous effect because the animals cannot get enough of it.

Have complaints been
received of animals being poisoned by chewing sacks which held the poison?

There was one
such case.
I know of one case in my district where that occurred.

I understood there were
complaints made in Alberta and other provinces because of animals having access to the empty sacks.
There was one such case in Alberta.

Does the department
contribute to the cost of destroying these pests?

No; the cost of
the. poison is paid on a fifty-fifty basis by the provincial government and the municipality. We supply the staff and assist in an advisory way.	*
